hits.subject: water
hits.title: Study and Interpretation of the Chemical Characteristics of Natural Water (Hem, USGS Water-Supply Paper 1473)
hits.text:
Fresh water density is close to 1 gram per millilitre, and it depends on temperature and on what
is dissolved. The report says "The density is usually determined to three decimal places, and the
temperature at which it was made (usually 20°C) is given." It also says "The density of a water is
a significant physical property that affects its behavior in natural systems".

hits.subject: water
hits.title: Study and Interpretation of the Chemical Characteristics of Natural Water (Hem, USGS Water-Supply Paper 1473)
hits.text:
A litre of water weighs 1 kilogram only near 4 degrees Celsius. The report says "This assumption
is strictly true only for pure water at 3.89° C." It adds "The presence of dissolved mineral matter
tends to increase the density, and at higher temperatures the density decreases."

content.text:
The density of **Polymaker PolyTerra PLA+ is 1.24 g/cm³ at 21.5 °C**, measured to ISO 1183 / GB/T 1033.

**Source:** *PolyTerra PLA+ technical data sheet V5.1* (Polymaker), page 2, physical properties table, "Density ISO1183, GB/T1033 1.24 g/cm3 at 21.5°C".
https://cdn.shopify.com/s/files/1/0789/2979/files/PolyTerra_PLA_Plus_EN_V5.1.pdf (retrieved 2026-11-07)

**Don't mix it up with plain PolyTerra PLA.** The plain grade has its own data sheet (*PolyTerra PLA TDS V6.0*, page 1), which gives **1.31 g/cm³ at 23 °C**. That's about 6% higher. Check which spool you have.

**Mass checks on your bracket:** PolyTerra PLA+ isn't in the materials table that the scoring tool uses, so it can't calculate the bracket's mass in this material. The closest entries are other PLAs, such as `prusament-pla` and `bambu-pla-basic`, but their densities are different. I can also work out the mass by hand from 1.24 g/cm³ once a scorecard gives the volume, but that number would be my own arithmetic, not a check.

The density comes from Polymaker's data sheet, and nothing in this toolset has checked it. It's a candidate value until you confirm it. A printed part also usually weighs less than its solid volume × density, because of infill and perimeter settings.
